title: GraphQL resolver batching and cache invalidation overhaul to reduce Console API p99
creator: Priya Singh
description: Symptoms: Console user-facing API p99 token latency spikes during dashboard load (observed ~1.8s -> 3.5s under moderate load). Root causes identified in profiling: repeated small GraphQL resolver calls (N+1 patterns) for route /models/:id/usage, inefficient per-request cache invalidation, and a legacy Redis client pinned to an older connection model that amplifies tail latency. Goal: reduce p99 by 30-40% through targeted refactors: introduce DataLoader-style batching for the top 6 hot resolvers, centralize cache invalidation to a single coherent layer with event-driven TTL propagation, and upgrade redis client and graphql-js to latest LTS versions that include performance fixes.
acceptance_criteria: Console p99 for /v1/console/graphql end-to-end: reduce from baseline 3.5s to <=2.2s on the same load profile (JMeter scenario: 200 concurrent users, 6s think time).
GraphQL resolver traces show >70% fewer resolver calls per request for the affected queries (confirmed in Zipkin/Jaeger).
Cache invalidation unit tests + integration tests cover user, org, and route-level TTL propagation; no stale reads in >1000 synthetic updates run in CI.
Node/npm dependency upgrades merged and deployed with no regression to existing GraphQL schema or auth flows; automated smoke tests pass in staging.
Documentation: Confluence RFC updated, and Runbook entry added for cache invalidation incidents.
implementation_plan: Stage 1: Add a lightweight batching layer (DataLoader abstraction) to top hot resolvers (routes, billing usage, token-allocations). Toggle behind feature flag `graphql-batching-v2`.
Stage 2: Replace per-resolver cache invalidation calls with a single CacheManager that subscribes to domain events (user.update, route.deploy). Implement event dedup window and TTL bumping strategy.
Stage 3: Upgrade dependencies: graphql-js 18.x -> 20.x, node 18 -> 20 (evaluate), ioredis 4.x -> 6.x. Bench test runtime heap and connection pooling under load.
Stage 4: Add tracing and per-resolver metrics (histograms + percentiles) in instrumentation; wire into existing Grafana dashboards.
Stage 5: Canary deploy to staging -> canary prod (10% traffic) -> full rollout; monitor p99, error-rates, and GC/CPU.
Stage 6: Postmortem and knowledge share: update RFC and host brownbag for platform and consumer teams.
notes: Early profiling (2026-02-12): top offender resolvers executed ~12-30 extra DB/HTTP calls per request due to missing batching.
Experiment: simple DataLoader implementation reduced resolver calls by 8x in local bench for /models query. Need to validate with full stack and auth token overhead.
Risk: Node upgrade may change native http/keepalive behavior; we will run soak tests for 48h on staging before canary.
Fallback plan: feature-flag off and automatic rollback policy if p99 increases >10% or error-rate >2% above baseline during canary.
